extracted.intended_audience: government contracting officers, federal procurement attorneys, contractors and legal practitioners advising on U.S. federal contract/appropriations law
extracted.subtask_description: Legal/practical standards for making, interpreting, and enforcing contracts by or with the United States, focusing on limitations imposed by annual and permanent appropriations, exceptions for military purchases, apportionment rules, assignment restrictions, and related statutory provisions (secs. 3679, 3732, 3733, 3737 R.S.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on contracts binding future payments beyond appropriations (sec. 3679)
rubrics_metrics.description: All contracts, based on an annual appropriation, by which the Government may be bound for the future payment of any moneys in excess of the appropriations of the fiscal year are unauthorized and incapable of being enforced at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracts that purport to bind the United States to payments in future fiscal years are void unless specifically authorized by statute. Example: a contract purportedly for a 'calendar year' that spans two fiscal years is unauthorized. Where practicable, contracts should run concurrently with the fiscal year. Citation: R. 31, 40; R. 31, 392; R. 35, 613.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leases and multi‑year obligations funded by annual appropriations
rubrics_metrics.description: A lease made for a term of years (e.g., three, five, ninety‑nine years), the rent of which is payable out of an annual appropriation, is inoperative to bind the Government beyond the fiscal year unless specially authorized by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indefinite-term leases payable from annual appropriations are similarly ineffective past the fiscal year. When premises are needed beyond one year under an annual appropriation, take a lease only to the end of the current fiscal year and renew by new lease each year. Exceptions exist where no rent or only nominal rent is reserved (military necessity) or where statute makes appropriation permanent or otherwise authorizes multi‑year commitment. Authorities: McCallum's case; R. 32, 642; 42, 677; 36, 315.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions for permanent appropriations and express statutory authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an appropriation is permanent (available 'until expended') or a statute expressly authorizes contracting without annual limitation, contracts may lawfully cover a period longer than the current fiscal year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: statute authorizing up to $2M annually for arms remaining available until expended permitted a five‑year lease with reservations and termination options. When statute authorizes whole project without cost restriction, government may contract for the entire project though payments limited by available Treasury funds; subsequent appropriations can fund completion. Citations: C. 14919; C. 19798; 34 Stat. 449.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military/naval purchases exception (sec. 3732) — current fiscal year limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Military and naval contracts for clothing, subsistence, forage, fuel, quarters, transportation (and medical/hospital supplies by later act) may be entered into irrespective of adequacy of appropriations, but shall not exceed the necessities of the current year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Current year' is to be understood as the current fiscal year; military authorities can bind the Government only for necessary supplies for that fiscal year. This exception allows purchases on credit when appropriations are omitted, but limits duration/amount to current fiscal needs. Authorities: R. 38, 503; C. 26334.

rubrics_metrics.name: No contract without authorization by law or adequate appropriation (sec. 3732/3733)
rubrics_metrics.description: No contract or purchase on behalf of the United States shall be made unless it is authorized by law or is under an appropriation adequate to its fulfillment; no contract shall bind the Government to pay a larger sum than the amount in the Treasury appropriated for the specific purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two cases: (1) express statutory authorization permits contracting for entire project (but payments limited to Treasury funds available); (2) where power to contract arises solely from an appropriation, the power is limited by that appropriation and contracts in excess are void. Contracts contingent on future appropriations cannot bind the Government to future payments. Authorities: Chase v. U.S.; 15 Op. Atty. Gen.; Bradley v. U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts contingent upon future appropriations are void to bind future funds
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract that attempts to bind the Government to future appropriations (e.g., stating it is contingent on later appropriations) will not be binding so far as to attach to future appropriations even if such appropriations are later made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clause making the contract dependent on a future appropriation does not render the contract valid as to those future monies; the government cannot be bound in advance of appropriation. Authorities: 15 Op. Atty. Gen. 235; Bradley v. U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for 'extras' depends on scope of authorization and nature of appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract is authorized without restriction as to cost, the Government will be liable for extra work and materials accepted. Where a contract is made under a general appropriation, the Government may be liable for extras; but if the contract on its face covers all work authorized by an appropriation, the contractor is bound to know the appropriation amount and cannot exceed it by doing extras.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contract language and the source/nature of appropriation determine whether extras are payable. Case authorities: 2 Ct. Cls. 151; 16 id. 528; others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment of appropriations (sec. 3679) and supervisory duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriations for contingent or general purposes shall, on or before the beginning of each fiscal year, be apportioned by monthly or other allotments to prevent undue expenditures in one portion of the year; apportionments must be adhered to except when waived or modified in specific cases by written order of the department head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apportionment may be monthly, quarterly, unequal, or mixed; amounts need not be uniform across units. The head of the department must supervise adherence and may be responsible for preventing exceedance; disbursing officers are generally not charged with duty except where they disburse entire appropriations. Bills incurred in one period in excess of apportionment may be paid in a later period provided payment is within the fiscal year. Authorities: C. 18240; C. 18240 (July 11, 1905); C. 18240 (Feb. 2, 1906).

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary service prohibition and emergency exception (sec. 3679)
rubrics_metrics.description: No department or officer shall accept voluntary service or employ personal service in excess of that authorized by law, except in cases of sudden emergency involving loss of human life or destruction of property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Voluntary service' under sec. 3679 means service rendered with the understanding that a claim for payment may subsequently be made; services rendered in wartime or great public emergency by authorized private societies (e.g., Red Cross), civilian physicians, nurses, etc., without expectation of reimbursement, are not within the prohibition. Authorities: C. 20866; C. 20916; XI Comp. Dec. 622.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on creating moral/imperfect obligations to evade appropriation limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive officers cannot lawfully enter agreements that create moral or 'imperfect' obligations intended to be a ground for subsequent appropriations; without Congressional authority, such commitments are unauthorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracts conditioning payment upon later appropriation or that leave the Government morally obligated (though not legally) to pay are prohibited; intended to prevent creating pressures for supplemental appropriations. Authority: C. 19401 (Mar. 10, 1904).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising for bids when appropriation lacking
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is no adequate appropriation applicable to the subject, there can be neither a contract nor an award or acceptance of a bid until an adequate appropriation exists; it is proper (though not necessary) to notify bidders of the lack of appropriation in solicitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising for bids in the absence of appropriation is permitted provided award/contract only follows appropriation; include clause notifying bidders to avoid misunderstanding. Authority: R. 50, 338.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on contracts involving indefinite, uncertain future liabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts proposing to make the Government liable for indefinite and uncertain sums that cannot be definitely ascertained at the time of contracting are unauthorized and void under sec. 3679 as amended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obligations contingent upon undeterminable future events (e.g., payment of damages whose amount depends on future facts) are impracticable to fund from appropriations and therefore lack legal authority. Authority: C. 27468.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on using retained/reserved sums to pay unappropriated work
rubrics_metrics.description: Amounts reserved (e.g., contract retainage such as 10%) cannot be applied to pay for work not yet appropriated; doing so would indirectly pay for work in advance of appropriation and violate appropriations rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contract clauses reserving a percentage to be paid later cannot be used as a device to fund work beyond appropriated amounts; courts held such application would violate the contract's and statute's limitations. Authority: C. 620 (Nov. 15, 1894).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificates of indebtedness and disbursing officers' limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Disbursing officers should not issue undertakings that operate as certificates of indebtedness or 'due bills' against the United States; issuance of such vouchers is disapproved except narrow exceptions (e.g., certified statements for discharged employees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is allowable to advise a vendor of purchase incidents and reasons for nonpayment; the Secretary of War may authorize paymasters to make a certificate in a specified form stating funds are not available. Practice of issuing due bills generally disapproved. Authority: G.O. 77, A.G.O. July 24, 1873; C. 25789.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clause drafting re: assignment (sec. 3737) — suggested wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Although sec. 3737 provides that transfer of a contract 'shall cause the annulment of the contract so far as the United States is concerned,' it is preferable to draft contract language stating that 'in case of such transfer the United States may refuse to carry out this contract either with the transferor or the transferee.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substituting the suggested wording more clearly expresses the statute's intended effect (government option to refuse performance) and avoids implying absolute abrogation as between private parties. Authority: C. 2878 (Jan. 19, 1897).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of assignment under sec. 3737 — voidable, not absolutely void
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment of a Government contract does not render it absolutely void as to private parties; it renders the contract voidable at the option of the United States, and acceptance of performance from the assignee ratifies the assignment so that payment may be made to the assignee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government may recognize and accept assignee (including surety who completes work) and pay assignee; acceptance or part performance by government ratifies assignment. However, officers cannot in advance recognize proposed assignments without proper authority. Partnership or subcontracting to furnish materials is not ordinarily an assignment. Authorities: 15 Op. Atty. Gen.; Burck v. Taylor; P. 16, 'l; C. 2933; C. 11328.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance by surety and payment to assignee
rubrics_metrics.description: If contractor defaults and surety completes the work and demonstrates assignment of contractor's rights to it, payments due (including retained percentages upon completion) may be paid to the surety/assignee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of assignment (voluntary or involuntary) to surety supports payment to surety; such assignment falls outside the mischief of sec. 3737. Authority: C. 11328; cases cited re: surety performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts with covenants creating future obligations (e.g., rebuild/maintenance) require reserved appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: A lease or contract that contains covenants obligating the Government to rebuild or perform future maintenance (creating future payment obligations) is not legal unless a sufficient sum from applicable appropriation is reserved or set aside to meet that future obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without setting aside funds to satisfy the covenant, there is no 'appropriation adequate to its fulfillment' and the contract is unauthorized. Example: lease of pier with covenant to rebuild unless funds reserved would be illegal. Authority: C. 12360; C. 5089.
